topics.title: 2.1.1 The Objectives of Government Economic Policy

cards.front: State the four main objectives of government macroeconomic policy in the AQA specification.
cards.back:
Economic growth; price stability (low and stable inflation — the UK's 2% CPI target); minimising unemployment; and a stable balance of payments on current account.

AQA also expects awareness of further objectives — balancing the government budget, a more equitable distribution of income, and environmental protection — and that the importance attached to each objective changes over time.

cards.front: Give the UK's usual targets for growth, unemployment and inflation, and why each matters.
cards.back:
Growth — sustainable, around 2–3%: raises incomes, living standards, employment and tax revenue. Unemployment — near full employment, around 4–5%, allowing for frictional unemployment: maximises output and reduces poverty. Inflation — the 2% CPI target: certainty for consumers and firms, protects savings, supports competitiveness.

The current account aim is a sustainable position — only a small surplus or deficit.

cards.front: Why can the macroeconomic objectives conflict, at least in the short run?
cards.back:
Policies that improve one objective often worsen another: stimulating growth and employment raises demand-pull inflation and pulls in imports; squeezing inflation with higher interest rates slows growth and costs jobs.

Governments therefore prioritise, and the priority shifts with circumstances — jobs and demand after 2008, inflation in 2022–23. AQA flags exactly this: the importance attached to objectives changes over time.

cards.front: Distinguish nominal GDP, real GDP and real GDP per capita.
cards.back:
Nominal GDP values output at current prices; real GDP adjusts for inflation, valuing output at constant prices — approximately, % change in real GDP = % change in nominal GDP − inflation.

Real GDP per capita divides real GDP by the population: average output per person, the better starting point for living standards.

cards.front: How does the RPI differ from the CPI?
cards.back:
Both track the average change in prices of a basket of goods and services and are used to calculate the inflation rate. The RPI additionally includes housing costs — mortgage interest payments and council tax — which the CPI leaves out.

RPI therefore usually runs higher than CPI, and the CPI is the measure targeted by the Bank of England.

cards.front: State the formulas for the unemployment rate and the employment rate.
cards.back:
The unemployment rate is the percentage of the labour force unemployed and actively seeking work. The employment rate is the percentage of the working-age population in work.

The denominators differ — someone economically inactive is in neither numerator, so the two rates can move independently.

cards.front: Define the current account of the balance of payments, and name the remaining spec indicator.
cards.back:
The balance of payments records all transactions between a country and the rest of the world; the current account is the part that records trade in goods and services, income flows, and current transfers.

The final indicator on the AQA list is productivity — output per worker (or per hour worked) — which drives long-run growth and competitiveness.

An index number expresses the value of a variable relative to a chosen base value, which is set equal to 100. The base year is the reference year all others are compared against.

Index numbers turn awkward raw figures — thousands of prices, GDP in billions — into one easy series, and they track not just prices but real GDP, wages, productivity and share prices such as the FTSE 100.

cards.front: State the index number formula, and interpret an index of 115.
cards.back: An index of 115 means the variable is 15% higher than in the base year; an index of 92 means 8% lower. The percentage change reads straight off the index only against the base year — comparing 115 with 105 is a rise of 115 ÷ 105, about 9.5%, not 10 points.

cards.front: Why does the CPI use weights, and what do the 'average family' and the 'basket' mean?
cards.back:
The CPI prices a basket of goods and services chosen to represent the spending of the average family. Each category gets a weight reflecting its share of household spending, so a 10% rise in a heavily-weighted item (housing) moves the index far more than the same rise in a lightly-weighted one (tea bags).

The weighted index is the sum of weight × price index across categories, divided by the total weight.

cards.front: A simplified basket has three categories with weights out of 1,000: housing 400 (price index 108), transport 350 (index 104), food 250 (index 112). Calculate the weighted CPI and interpret it.
cards.back:
Weight × index: housing 400 × 108 = 43,200; transport 350 × 104 = 36,400; food 250 × 112 = 28,000.

Total = 107,600; divide by total weight: 107,600 ÷ 1,000 = 107.6

Prices across the basket average 7.6% above the base year. Food rose fastest (12%), but the heavily-weighted housing category matters more to the overall index — that is what weighting does.

cards.front: Define national income, and state the national income identity.
cards.back:
National income is the total value of all goods and services produced in an economy over a given period. It can be measured in three equivalent ways — as total output, total income, or total expenditure — because one person's spending is another person's income, and all income is ultimately earned by producing output.

Hence the identity: national output ≡ national income ≡ national expenditure.

GDP measures the value of everything produced within a country's borders, regardless of who owns the factors of production.

GNI (also called GNP) is GDP plus net income from abroad — income earned by residents from overseas assets, minus income earned by foreign residents from domestic assets. For countries with large overseas holdings or heavy inward investment, the two diverge noticeably.

cards.front: Evaluate the limitations of national income data for comparing living standards.
cards.back:
Even real GDP per capita hides much: income distribution (an average conceals inequality); the informal economy (subsistence farming, unpaid care, the hidden economy go unrecorded — a big understatement in developing countries); quality of life (health, leisure, freedom); negative externalities (polluting output still counts); the composition of output (defence spending raises GDP without raising welfare); and data reliability across countries.

The fullest single comparison is real GDP per capita at PPP; broader indices such as the HDI add health and education.

cards.front: What is purchasing power parity, and why does it matter for international comparisons?
cards.back:
PPP is an exchange rate that equalises the price of an identical basket of goods and services between two countries — what a currency actually buys at home, not what it trades for on foreign exchange markets.

Market rates mislead because they are driven by currency demand and supply, and because non-traded goods — housing, haircuts, restaurant meals — tend to be cheaper in lower-income countries. Comparing incomes at market rates therefore understates living standards in poorer economies.
